title: Straight unit conversion (one or chained factors)
subtitle: Ratios, rates, proportional relationships, and units · 18 official questions

sections.heading: Where this sits for you
body: **18 of the official questions in Ratios, rates, proportional relationships, and units are this one** — 13 Easy, 5 Medium, 0 Hard.
It is bottom-heavy, which makes it cheap points. Secure it early.

sections.heading: How to spot it
body: You are looking at this pattern when:
- The question asks 'how many [unit B] are equivalent to [amount] [unit A]?', or gives a measurement and asks for it in another unit.
- There is no rate or story to model, only a quantity in one unit.
- Sometimes the question supplies the conversion factor.
- Sometimes it expects you to know a standard one (feet in a yard, inches in a yard, cups in a quart).
- If the two units are far apart, it may give a middle unit to chain through.

sections.heading: The method
body: - 1) Write the amount as a fraction and multiply by conversion fractions set up so each unwanted unit cancels, with the old unit in the denominator and the new unit in the numerator.
- 2) If the units are far apart, chain two factors through the middle unit.
- 3) Sanity-check the direction: going to a smaller unit should give a bigger number.

sections.heading: Where Desmos fits
body: It barely helps.
The work is setting up the factor chain, not solving anything.
You can type the whole product as a line to avoid arithmetic slips, but getting the direction right is on you.

sections.heading: What it is built to catch
body: You divide when you should multiply, or the reverse, and land on the choice that converts the wrong way.
That choice is almost always offered.
The other trap is using the wrong standard factor from memory, such as 3 inches per foot or 12 inches per yard, or stopping after the first factor in a two-step chain.

sections.heading: You are losing these
body: Before you choose, say out loud what the question is asking for — not what you solved for.
You divide when you should multiply, or the reverse, and land on the choice that converts the wrong way.
That choice is almost always offered.
